approach.method_basis: The Parent trains a recurrent SMILES language prior on the allowed unlabeled molecules and starts each objective with a fresh policy copied from that frozen prior. Each accepted batch contributes its best-scoring half, joined by the strongest eligible historical records from a memory of thirty-two accepted elites. The original accepted strings and scores are retained. Historical row weights decrease with the number of earlier fitting batches that used each identity, then are rescaled to preserve the total historical loss share; current elites keep equal coefficients. The policy fits these weighted rows toward frozen-prior log likelihood plus sixty times accepted reward, using squared residuals and up to twelve clipped Adam steps. The final policy directly samples complete SMILES, with chemical validation and canonical duplicate rejection refilling the announced batch.
approach.novelty: Add a Huber residual penalty to bound the influence of unusually large likelihood errors. Errors within one natural-log probability unit retain the Parent quadratic penalty; larger errors receive a linear penalty, so their scalar learning influence stops growing while its direction is preserved. The existing fitting-exposure weights still determine each row’s coefficient. This addresses unequal influence caused by error magnitude inside the already selected learning group. The earlier siblings changed historical access, fitting-exposure weights, target normalization, checkpoint retention or historical update protection. None bounded residual influence while preserving the augmented targets. Same-state gradient comparisons will test whether this changes the direction actually passed through gradient clipping to Adam. Useful subsequent molecules, completion reliability and paired scores remain separate tests of value.

nodes.hypothesis: Replace each selected row’s squared augmented-likelihood residual with the Huber penalty rho(r)=r^2 for abs(r)<=1 and rho(r)=2*abs(r)-1 otherwise, preserving the Parent exposure coefficients, fixed augmented targets and training membership, so the scalar likelihood-gradient factor becomes -2*q_i*clamp(r_i,-1,1) instead of -2*q_i*r_i.

finding_summary.headline: Huber bounding changed clipped gradients, but endpoint scores fell despite faster early progress.
finding_summary.insights:
Residual bounding survives global gradient clipping as a directional change; the result rules out the explanation that clipping simply erases it as a common rescaling. Yet reducing scalar concentration and slightly reducing historical row regressions did not produce broader useful search. Faster discovery on a task already near its score ceiling can improve average AUC while substantial losses elsewhere lower final quality. The chemistry assessment is consistent with this split: strong amine-rich families coexist with repeated analogue families, scattered winners on the weakest task, uneven attachment chemistry and unresolved stereochemistry. Those observations do not identify which chemical limitation caused the score loss.

The bound also leaves the target problem intact: positive, individually unattainable targets occur in 1,243 nonterminal selected-row appearances, versus 988 for the parent. Their scalar influence is reduced, but their feasibility is unchanged. Whether useful large residuals were damped too strongly remains open; these runs do not isolate initialization, upward versus downward pressure, or individual chemical families as the cause. Six updates began entirely in the quadratic region and matched the original gradient exactly, then entered the Huber tail during later Adam steps. Starting-state equality is therefore a narrower control than whole-update equality. Recorded sequence likelihoods support these conclusions, but token-level probability changes and forgetting between unobserved appearances remain unmeasured.
finding_summary.results:
The Huber rule changed the learning direction after clipping at all 429 nonterminal starts with tail residuals. On those comparisons, its mean gradient cosine with the original squared-error objective was 0.888. Across the child's 435 nonterminal starting tensors, the original objective's two largest scalar factors held 52.66% of absolute influence on average; those same rows held 33.20% under Huber. All 53,100 actual-step row derivatives obeyed the registered bound and all 450 first backward passes matched the direct Huber gradient. In the 420 history-bearing nonterminal updates, mean weighted Huber loss fell from 13.588 to 9.621. Historical row errors worsened in 863 of 2,100 appearances, compared with 906 for the parent.

All 15 task runs completed their 300-evaluation budgets. Mean endpoint score fell from 0.517655 to 0.500773; the paired mean change was -0.016882, with seed changes -0.023903, +0.004450 and -0.031193. The largest task loss was sitagliptin_mpo (-0.088317), followed by deco_hop (-0.009741); zaleplon_mpo improved by 0.012418, drd2_docking by 0.001297, and median_2 was nearly unchanged (-0.000067). Recorded mean AUC rose from 0.406769 to 0.448820, chiefly through earlier drd2_docking progress. Raw duplicate draws rose from 36.22% to 38.41%, and distinct chemical-core counts fell in four of five tasks. The predicted endpoint gain of at least 0.002 was therefore not achieved.

No candidate import, learned-state reconstruction, model forward, optimizer, smoke/evaluation, molecule generation or new oracle score is executed.

Each task log has objective initialization at line 1, 30 update receipts at lines 2,5,...,89, and 29 actual generation receipts at lines 4,7,...,88. Update 29 at line 89 is terminal. Child seed-0 logs/zaleplon_mpo.log line 5 supplies a concrete historical activation witness: first current row residual 15.600360870361328, q=0.1, Parent scalar factor -3.120072174072266, Huber factor -0.2, measured autograd factor -0.20000000298023224. The same-state clipped Huber/MSE gradient difference is 0.6631616306639336, cosine 0.7801083154914085, orthogonal difference 0.6256444563829838 against tolerance 1.0099999917873192e-6; the real first backward differs from Huber by exactly zero. Child seed-0 logs/sitagliptin_mpo.log line 2 starts with exact zero Huber/MSE gradient difference but enters a two-row tail at actual step two. The audit retains all six such initial-state controls and excludes them from starting-state direction activation.

Numerical qualification: nine Huber group-summation comparisons exceed the registered full-vector tolerance, maximum 1.1613564605252873 times tolerance at child seed-1 drd2_docking update 2 (log line 8): difference 5.026991214399332e-5 versus tolerance 4.328551469998797e-5. This is a separately differentiated group-combination discrepancy; direct Huber-versus-real-backward differences are zero in all 450 updates. The inherited passive MSE combination records additionally have six Child and 31 Parent discrepancies. No historical full gradient vectors or RNG/optimizer snapshots were invented; source purity and existing buffer receipts establish diagnostic scope.

Formal summary.json and run.log pairs provide every endpoint score and recorded AUC. run.log lines 4-9 hold status, task scores, oracle count, macro score, seed and batch size. All per-task logs and trajectories, their hashes and exact receipt line lists are recorded under audit.json sessions; the six replica manifests and prepared identities are recorded under replicas.

molecular.headline: Ring-rich medicinal chemistry with recurring analogue families, uneven attachment chemistry and no specified stereochemistry.
molecular.overall_character:
Node n-0a6bb09846c7 produces predominantly medium-sized aromatic and heteroaromatic molecules, often joined to amides, sulfonamides or saturated nitrogen rings. The full trajectories also contain tiny fragments, extended alkyl chains, peptide-like assemblies and unusual nitrogen linkages. All five objectives are covered: tasks_without_trajectories is empty. Each digest covers 900 recorded molecules, including 870 optimizer proposals. Across the tasks, the digest's proposal-level ring-closure rates run from 0.9655 to 0.9954 and aromatic-token presence from 0.9218 to 0.9931; these are string-presence rates, not fractions of atoms. Ring chemistry and common medicinal functional groups are already abundant. Many individual structures look synthetically conventional, but the entire stream merits a questionable plausibility rating because connectivity, molecular size and stereochemical definition are uneven. Diversity is moderate overall: numerous distinct cores coexist with strongly repeated late analogue families in individual seeds.

A passive RDKit reading of all 30 named Child/Parent trajectories, totaling 9,000 recorded rows, is saved in /projects/standard/adeshwal/shared/zhou2577/SPIRAL/runs/SPIRAL2/policy/responses/r0011-00-improve-L03-molecular.audit.json, with its reproducible .audit.py beside it. All 4,350 Child optimizer records parse, which establishes graph validity only. RDKit detects unspecified tetrahedral centres in 1,235 Child records versus 827 Parent records; neither set contains an assigned tetrahedral centre. The digest independently reports stereocentre_rate 0.0 on every task. Formal charge tokens include groups such as nitro and nitrate and cannot be read as protonated-amine coverage. Descriptor and substructure counts below are passive calculations from the shown trajectories, not new objective scores or synthesis predictions. The digest's final_molecules excerpt comes from the concatenated seed stream's tail; statements about other seeds use their full trajectories. Parent comparisons describe observed chemical differences without attributing them to a mechanism.

per_task.generated_character: The high-scoring region contains compact aromatic carbonyl compounds with nitriles: a methoxy/cyano pyrrole carrying an N-carbamoyl group with N-benzyl and N-phenyl substitution, related aza-ring variants, and cyanopyridyl piperazines capped with aromatic amides. The first cited molecule has 25 heavy atoms and three aromatic rings; the cited benzofuran-carbonyl piperazine has 25 heavy atoms and four rings. Seed 2 instead develops tertiary aryl amides with diaryl sulfide or diarylamine connections. These are recognizable synthetic building-block combinations, although the N-carbamoylated aromatic nitrogen and occasional N-N substitution require more scrutiny than a conventional carboxamide. Relative to Parent n-3462511d7ff0, nitrile-bearing optimizer records increase from 7 to 135 while median heavy-atom count remains 24; the Parent's leading pyrrole/aryl-amide families largely lacked nitriles.
liabilities: The worst large polyaryl carbamate has extensive flexible aromatic bulk and an unspecified stereocentre; its valid SMILES does not establish a practical synthesis or useful physical properties.

A high-scoring relative replaces the benzyl substituent with an N-N-linked anilino group, scoring 0.4688756433021988. That change creates different chemical reactivity and attachment chemistry, not merely a cosmetic token substitution.
missing_features: Consistent co-presentation of the compact cyano/heteroaryl and carbonyl arrangements seen in the highest-scoring region: the final seed-2 amides omit the nitrile, and both deletion and expansion can leave very low scores. This is a failure to retain a useful combination, not an absence of aromatic rings or amides.

The examples do not identify a uniquely required fused ring or exact target structure. Ring-nitrogen substitutions produce different observed scores, leaving the attachment and acceptor arrangement unresolved even within the compact family.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The cyano/methoxy N-carbamoylpyrrole scores 0.5080243269702821, and its aza-ring variants score 0.49951771119270083 and 0.4791144732035122. The cyanopyridyl piperazine/benzofuran amide reaches 0.4768911921899254. The lowest cited carbamate/amide assembly has 53 heavy atoms, six aromatic rings and 15 rotatable bonds, yet scores 8.727792954487862e-40. Conversely, the small final diaryl carboxamide scores only 0.0025033045090448055, so simply shrinking molecules does not explain success. The observed preference is for a bounded aromatic framework with an appropriate arrangement of acceptor and carbonyl groups. The initial methoxyindole carboxamide already scores 0.3051048083696145. Parent's strongest recorded molecule reaches 0.4902347642636414; the Child finds a different cyano-bearing family rather than a uniform improvement of all Parent families.

per_task.generated_character: The strongest digest examples are heavily fluorinated polyheteroaryls: a triazine/quinoline/phenyl assembly and fused imidazole-type heterocycles bearing thiazole or triazole substituents. The first cited structure has 32 heavy atoms and five aromatic rings. Other seeds occupy benzylamino arylsulfonamide and quinazolinone/sulfonamide families; the final seed-2 examples add fluoroalkyl chains, aminoethyl substituents and fused aryl ethers. These contain familiar coupling and sulfonamide motifs, but the fluorination and long substituents create substantial chemical bulk. Parent's repeated nonaromatic nitrogen-chain chemistry recedes: records with a nonaromatic N-N single bond fall from 236 to 18, while sulfonamide-bearing records rise from 160 to 366. The Child still repeats whole core families; its largest Murcko family contains 143 proposals.
liabilities: The top polyheteroaryls have extensive aromatic surface and repeated halogens, with little saturated three-dimensional structure; solubility and physical behaviour remain unmeasured.

The quinazolinone/sulfonamide tail adds flexible fluoroalkyl chains without a consistent score advantage. Graph-valid tiny nitrate or hydrocarbon outputs are chemically remote from the useful ring-rich families.
missing_features: Reliable transfer of the useful heteroaryl and sulfonamide attachment geometry across distinct cores. The ingredients appear repeatedly, but altered connections and long peripheral chains do not reproduce the highest-scoring combinations.

There is no demonstrated missing universal halogen or ring count: adjacent fluorination variants and identical chloro/bromo scores show limited guidance from those changes. The remaining structural requirement cannot be resolved from score and SMILES alone.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The leading polyheteroaryl scores 0.6093686902678692. An additional fluorinated analogue scores 0.607979157511457, and the cited chloro/bromo imidazole-type analogues both score exactly 0.6062250142775557, so adding or swapping halogens is not reliably rewarded. Tiny ethene scores 0.5 and nitrate 0.5004402958788305; those baselines do not indicate medicinal quality. A larger quinazolinone with an N-C-S(=O)2 attachment scores 0.3404510410975536, whereas the final direct N-S(=O)2 sulfonamide example scores 0.5842942636111517. These also differ in substituents, so this is evidence of attachment sensitivity rather than a controlled bond-edit effect. Parent's strongest recorded polyheteroaryl reaches 0.6186220344491388. The Child changes the chemical families without establishing a superior replacement arrangement from these molecules alone.

per_task.generated_character: The high-scoring output is rich in unacylated saturated ring amines and hydrophobic aromatic domains. Seed 1 produces arylcyclohexyl chains connected through secondary amines to pyridylpiperazines; the leading cited molecule has 30 heavy atoms, two aromatic rings and two saturated rings. Seed 0 produces N-pentyl arylpiperazines attached to heavily substituted benzophenones, including iodine, methoxy and aniline groups. Seed 2 finishes with N-phenethyl piperidine/azepane compounds carrying pyridyl or pyrazole/indole substituents. Much of this is recognizable medicinal chemistry with plausible bond constructions, although no routes were demonstrated. Parent already generated arylated saturated amines; the Child has 615 optimizer records with the audit's unacylated saturated-ring-N flag versus 524 in Parent, with different linker and aryl families.
liabilities: The leading cyclohexyl structure has two unspecified tetrahedral centres. Across this task, 441 optimizer records have an unspecified tetrahedral centre versus 218 in Parent, so apparent three-dimensional richness is accompanied by undefined stereochemistry.

Several strong examples combine long alkyl linkers, multiple potentially protonatable amines and heavy aryl halogenation. Exact score ties do not establish equal basicity, permeability, solubility or synthetic burden.
missing_features: No additional pharmacophore is demonstrated as missing from the highest-scoring structures: saturated ring amines and aromatic domains are already prominent. Their relative spatial arrangement is incompletely specified, particularly the stereoisomers of the substituted cyclohexane and piperidine compounds.

Evidence for compact, less flexible alternatives preserving the same productive amine-to-aromatic spacing is limited in the cited high-score families. The present scores do not establish that additional rings, halogens or charge centres would help.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The arylcyclohexyl/amine/piperazine example and its chloro relative both score 0.9999996838046051. The iodine-bearing benzophenone piperazine scores 0.9999991582889631, including a more heavily iodinated counterpart with the same value. Low examples instead contain amides, ester-linked carbonyls or sulfonamides without the freely basic saturated-ring arrangement, scoring 2.366998874472172e-05 and 3.8021829379963674e-05. These observations support an association with accessible amine centres appropriately separated from aromatic bulk, rather than polar nitrogen in general. Parent's strongest recorded example already scores 0.9999855104574086. The near-ceiling Child values and exact halogen ties leave little observed discrimination among some chemically different analogues; they establish neither binding geometry nor measured affinity.

per_task.generated_character: The strongest digest region is an arylsulfonyl-N-methylpiperazine series, decorated with alkoxy groups and either a biaryl or naphthalene aromatic domain. The leading ethoxy biaryl has 26 heavy atoms, two aromatic rings and one saturated piperazine ring; the ethoxy naphthalene analogue has 23 heavy atoms and three rings. These are among the more synthetically conventional examples shown, combining aryl ether, sulfonamide and tertiary amine functionality. Other seeds explore more elaborate fused heterocycles, but every best_molecules entry in this digest comes from seed 2. Parent's strong families also contain arylsulfonyl piperazines, including a bis-sulfonylated example, whereas the leading Child family retains an N-methyl amine.
liabilities: Long alkoxy substitution increases flexible hydrophobic content without matching the compact ethoxy biaryl score. Some lower examples add unusual nitrogen-oxygen functionality or long unsaturated chains.

The high digest concentrates in one seed and related substitution patterns despite broad core variation elsewhere; chemical novelty across the whole stream does not by itself show useful alternative families.
missing_features: Consistent assembly of the useful aromatic domain, alkoxy position and sulfonylated piperazine connection. The components exist, yet many proposals dilute them through alternate attachment patterns or extended side chains.

Strong examples outside the recurring sulfonyl-piperazine family are not demonstrated by the digest. The remaining desired molecular arrangement cannot be identified as one specific missing reference scaffold from the observed scores.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The ethoxy biaryl scores 0.26796506084501276, and ethoxy naphthalene scores 0.24666619845812315. On the same naphthalene core, extending ethoxy to butoxy lowers the recorded score to 0.23446177292342862. On the methylphenyl sulfonamide core, ethoxy scores 0.22682497934216347 and methoxy 0.215365246126974. A much longer heptyloxy biaryl reaches only 0.21784176029783497. Thus the gradient appears sensitive to the arrangement and extent of aromatic/alkoxy/sulfonyl-piperazine features; unrestricted chain growth is not the answer. Acyclic unsaturated amino alcohol and the final alkyl ether ester score 0.014537095115739513 and 0.02676864788430937. Parent's strongest recorded example reaches 0.2588686674995393; the Child's strongest structure remains within related sulfonamide chemistry.

per_task.generated_character: The high-scoring structures are chemically scattered. The leading pair contains an oxalyl-derived acylhydrazine attached to a thiol-bearing imine/anilino unit, with phenylethyl or thienylethyl substitution. The first has 24 heavy atoms, two phenyl rings and an unspecified tetrahedral centre. Other relatively strong examples include a carbonyl-rich pyrimidinone, fluorinated fused aza-heterocycles with alcohol or oxo/hydroxy groups, and a conventional acylhydrazone. These have familiar subfragments but no recurring complete architecture across seeds. The low tail includes flexible peptide/polyol-like molecules, long hydrophobic assemblies and large multifunctional aromatic chains. Parent also showed heterogeneous winners; its leading aminoalkyl acylsulfonamide/fluoroaryl example is replaced by the Child's acylhydrazine and aza-heterocycle families.
liabilities: The leading acylhydrazine is written with an N-N=C(S)-N linkage, leaving thiol/thione tautomerism and imine geometry relevant to its actual chemical identity; the separate acylhydrazone raises similar geometric questions. These are scrutiny points, not evidence that such molecules cannot be synthesized.

The low tail includes highly flexible, multifunctional and sometimes very large molecules whose stereo- and chemoselective synthesis would be substantially more involved than their valid graph representation suggests. The final large amide/sulfone/guanidine-containing assembly scores 8.134203705089738e-56.
missing_features: A reproducible compact arrangement that combines productive polarity, hydrophobic substitution and heterocycle or carbonyl placement across different chemical families. The ingredients appear individually, while the final seed-2 structures vary widely and mostly retain very small scores.

Defined tetrahedral stereochemistry and, in the imine-containing families, a clearly specified geometric/tautomeric form. These are chemical representation gaps; the available records contain no comparison establishing which stereoisomer or tautomer the objective would reward.

The evidence does not justify prescribing the known drug structure or its presumed binding features. The scored examples support a joint molecular-property/arrangement gap, with no isolated required missing group established.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The phenylethyl acylhydrazine scores 0.2366403198264186 and its thienyl counterpart 0.22930408034503125; the methoxyphenyl-substituted relative scores 0.12693646079687687. The carbonyl-rich pyrimidinone scores 0.20330697814108128, and fluorinated aza-heterocycles reach 0.1845140226743423 and 0.17537867367789264. In contrast, the cited peptide-like and flexible polyol/amide assemblies score exactly 0.0. The final small fused aza-ring example still scores only 4.0308306926655526e-05, so either compactness or heteroatom richness alone is insufficient. The digest's median 0.0 is rounded: the optimizer-only raw-trajectory median is 1.1302129485900989e-07. Parent's strongest recorded example reaches 0.32609684308650033. The visible local gradient favours some compact combinations of polar groups and hydrophobic substituents but does not reveal a single unambiguous missing pharmacophore.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Every digest reports stereocentre_rate 0.0. Passive perception finds unspecified tetrahedral centres in 1,235 of 4,350 Child optimizer records and no assigned centres; a leading substituted cyclohexane carries two unspecified centres, and a leading phenylethyl acylhydrazine carries one.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator does not specify tetrahedral stereochemistry even when the proposed graph contains stereogenic centres.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: A general molecular representation and proposal process would need to preserve and vary stereochemical assignments for graphs that require them. Use observed feedback to assess those alternatives; these trajectories do not establish a preferred configuration or a guaranteed score benefit.

transferable_gaps.evidence: A direct sulfonamide-bearing terminal compound scores 0.5842942636111517, while a related heterocyclic family with an intervening carbon in the N-C-S(=O)2 connection scores 0.3404510410975536. Cyano carbamoyl variants also move among ordinary carbon attachments, aromatic-nitrogen acylation and an N-N substituent. These comparisons contain other edits and do not isolate a single bond effect.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator does not reliably preserve functional-group attachment chemistry when recombining otherwise useful fragments.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Represent useful attachment environments as chemically meaningful connected units and explore alternative connections while retaining the rest of a candidate coherently. Graph validity alone does not preserve functional-group identity, reactivity or the arrangement that accompanied a useful observation.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Cited chloro/bromo heteroaryl analogues have the identical recorded score 0.6062250142775557, and fluoro/chloro arylcyclohexyl amines both score 0.9999996838046051. Another high-score list consists entirely of one seed of arylsulfonyl piperazine variants. Full trajectories contain other cores, but these examples show repeated substitution within productive families.
transferable_gaps.gap: Expansion of useful families often remains at the level of halogen swaps or side-chain homologues rather than reliable alternative core arrangements.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: A task-agnostic generator needs ways to vary the core and attachment geometry while preserving feedback-supported local chemistry. Judge new arrangements by their actual observations; neither a distinct SMILES nor a larger scaffold count establishes a useful chemical alternative.

transferable_gaps.evidence: A 25-heavy-atom cyano carbonyl compound scores 0.5080243269702821 whereas a 53-heavy-atom polyaryl carbamate scores 8.727792954487862e-40; a small diaryl carboxamide also scores only 0.0025033045090448055. On a shared sulfonyl-piperazine naphthalene core, ethoxy scores 0.24666619845812315 and butoxy 0.23446177292342862. Large flexible peptide/polyol assemblies occur with zero recorded scores.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator does not consistently retain the useful balance of molecular size, flexibility and jointly presented functional groups.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Support local size and linker changes that preserve the joint arrangement associated with useful accepted molecules, and allow feedback to determine where growth or simplification helps. These heterogeneous observations do not support a universal size cutoff, blanket deletion of polar groups or one fixed motif recipe.

nodes.method_name: Augmented Hill-Climb with a corpus-trained SMILES policy
nodes.method_thesis: Train a compact autoregressive SMILES prior solely on the supplied unlabeled corpus, then initialize a fresh policy from that prior for each objective. Use the initial observations and each subsequent scored batch to update only its highest-reward sequences with the Augmented Hill-Climb loss: fit policy log likelihood to frozen-prior log likelihood plus scaled observed reward. Sample complete molecules token by token from the updated policy, canonicalize them, and refill invalid or duplicate proposals by further generation. The corpus supplies language training, never a ranked molecular pool. Elite-conditioned policy updates should shift generation toward new high-scoring molecular combinations quickly enough to improve the benchmark's mean final Top-1. This is a small-budget transfer hypothesis, not a claim that published larger-budget gains carry over. The root uses the current scored batch; randomized historical replay is reserved for the first improvement. The anchor's elite augmented-likelihood mechanism is described by [Thomas et al.](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-022-00646-z).

approach.method_basis: The Parent fits a regularized linear score predictor to accepted molecules using counts of atom types, heavy-atom degrees and element-typed bonds. It selects a scored molecule, retains its surrounding graph and uses a mixed-integer program to construct a small, singly attached replacement tree. The program chooses atoms, bonds and an attachment site while enforcing chemical constraints and exact agreement between the optimized counts and the submitted molecule. Accepted feedback refits the predictor and influences later source selection. This construction works, but its separate count summaries can assign the same representation to molecules with different substitution arrangements and different observed scores.
approach.novelty: Add bond-order-resolved counts of the two endpoint degrees, where an atom's degree is its number of attached heavy atoms. These counts describe whether branching or substituted sites are adjacent, so some positional and branching variants that previously tied can receive different learned predictions. The added counts enter both the existing ridge predictor and the exact integer construction equations. This lineage has only its root so far; no sibling has tested this representation. The experiment asks whether this added structural distinction changes actual construction preferences and can make predictions more useful.

nodes.hypothesis: Augment the Parent's exact molecular count representation with bond-order-resolved counts of the unordered pair of endpoint heavy-atom degrees, and fit and optimize the existing accepted-only ridge predictor over this enlarged descriptor vector through exact MILP equations.

finding_summary.headline: Degree-pair counts changed construction preferences and raised final scores overall, with uneven task gains
finding_summary.insights:
This closes a specific representational gap: adjacency of branching and substituted sites can supply learned information that changes exact graph construction. The eleven choices between molecules with identical old descriptors are particularly clear evidence, because the added counts alone break those predictor ties. Exact descriptor agreement and correct attachment corrections rule out optimized-to-submitted mismatch as the explanation for the remaining prediction errors.

Predictive usefulness is still uneven. On the same emitted molecules and the same accepted training data, the augmented predictor reduced pooled prediction RMSE from the shadow legacy model's 0.055579 to 0.053050, but increased mean absolute error from 0.024969 to 0.025680. Its advantage in final best score therefore does not establish generally better predictions or search trajectories, especially with only one replica and unscored diagnostic alternatives. The molecular assessment finds that familiar inherited rings still carry many unusual heteroatom-halogen and heteroatom-chain appendages, alongside conventional high-scoring chemistry. These richer degree counts do not enforce functional-group compatibility or expand the ring-construction domain. Further evidence should separate reliability across replicas, remaining representation limits, and chemical compatibility; the observed gain does not settle any of them.
finding_summary.results:
The added counts separated 556 of 705 molecular pairs that the parent represented identically, including 507 of 625 pairs with unequal recorded scores. The learned distinctions affected construction: 145 feasible comparisons with the same-data legacy predictor produced 107 strict preference reversals and 11 legacy ties broken in favor of the molecule actually emitted. All 1,450 emitted molecules exactly matched all 468 optimized counts, and every batch completed.

On the single screening seed, mean final Top-1 rose from 0.286518 to 0.296789. Docking increased from 0.189601 to 0.284516, decoration hopping from 0.583606 to 0.589489, and median_2 from 0.175888 to 0.183910. Zaleplon slipped from 0.395373 to 0.394288, while sitagliptin fell from 0.088123 to 0.031740. Mean trajectory AUC decreased slightly, from 0.252148 to 0.250435. Of 1,389 predicted source improvements, 604 became observed improvements, compared with 578 of 1,400 in the parent. Average actual source-relative gain remained negative, at -0.006834 versus -0.006591. Total evaluation time increased from 435 to 714 seconds, including about 43 seconds for diagnostic comparisons.

molecular.headline: Inherited ring frameworks carry exotic pendant groups; ordinary indole amides and alkylated diones coexist with heteroatom-halogen chains.
molecular.overall_character: All supplied current and Parent trajectories were read. Every task has 300 recorded molecules, including 290 optimizer proposals, from seed 0; no task lacks trajectories. The products retain recognizable indole carboxamides, diaryl fused diones, biaryl chromenones, quinoline/piperidine conjugates, arylsulfonyl pyrrolidines and oxygen-rich polyacetals. Ring and branch SMILES rates are 1.0 on every task. Aromatic-bearing SMILES rates range from 0.6448 to 1.0, so abundant aromatic chemistry coexists with a nonaromatic polyacetal upper-score series. These are generally medium-to-large, substantially substituted molecules. Diversity is moderate across the supplied collection but much narrower within its upper-score families; much of the visible novelty is peripheral substitution on frameworks already present initially. Conventional alkyl, ether, amide, amine and carbonyl functionality coexists with terminal diazenes, nitrogen/oxygen chains, direct heteroatom-halogen bonds, persulfides and haloalkynes. The Parent comparison shows changes in these appendages and in the relative prominence of familiar families, without a corresponding general shift toward ordinary medicinal chemistry. Every proposal set has charged_rate 0.0 and stereocentre_rate 0.0. Those are absent SMILES annotations, not evidence that the structures lack ionizable groups or stereogenic centres. Synthetic plausibility and liabilities below are structural judgements, not measured stability, route feasibility or biological activity. Recorded scores are rounded for readability. No reference structures or objective-component scores were supplied, so an unseen target pharmacophore cannot be inferred.

per_task.generated_character: The upper-score molecules are medium-sized indole carboxanilides: a fused pyrrolic aromatic system joined through an amide to a phenyl group, usually with aryl fluorine and methoxy or short alkyl substitution. Evaluation 292 adds an aryl terminal diazene; 297 instead has a sulfur substituent directly on the amide nitrogen. The simpler analogue at 240 retains an ordinary amide, methoxy groups, a methyl substituent and aryl fluorine. The wider trajectory also contains biaryl chromenones and densely oxygenated, nonaromatic polyacetals. Mean SMILES length is 51.2, aromatic_atom_rate is 0.9138 and halogen_rate is 0.6897. The indole/amide cores are plausible synthetic targets in outline; the complete diazene-, nitrogen-sulfur- and sulfur-fluorine-decorated variants require substantially more chemical justification.
liabilities: The terminal diazene at 292 and direct amide-N-S linkage at 297 make the complete molecules less conventional than their indole carboxamide cores. Other upper examples add direct S-F or N-S-N functionality; a sulfur-fluorine bond here must not be confused with a conventional sulfone.

Oxygen-sulfur appendages recur in the final material. Together with the unassigned geometry of diazene/imine groups elsewhere, they leave chemical identity, compatibility and isolation questions that the scalar score does not answer.
The lower-score polyacetals contain elaborate oxygen-bearing stereogenic frameworks without explicit configurations.
missing_features: The current upper-score excerpt lacks the comparably successful conventional N-alkyl amide chemistry seen in the Parent maximum. An ordinary secondary amide is present at 240, so the gap is sustained coverage of simple amide substitution within the favorable indole arrangement, not absence of amides.

Different fused-ring heteroatom arrangements and alternative connections between aromatic units are not demonstrated by the cited high molecules. Their value remains untested; the observed scores identify a favorable local family, not a specific missing target scaffold.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The initial trimethoxy indole carboxamide at 9 scores 0.305105. The less extensively oxygenated indole series reaches 0.352934 at 240, 0.386927 at 297 and 0.394288 at 292. The modified polyacetal at 93 scores only 4.09806e-06, despite its substantial ring and heteroatom content. The observed distinction therefore includes aromatic framework and substituent arrangement, not ring abundance alone. Within the same sulfur-substituted amide series, replacing the indole methyl of 297 with fluorine in 299 changes 0.386927 to 0.204535. The final amino/bis(oxygen-sulfur)-substituted indole at 300 scores 0.127853. More halogen or heteroatom decoration is not uniformly favored. Parent n-edf80f0d6f5e reached 0.395373 with an ordinary N-methyl indole amide. The current maximum occupies a similar recorded neighborhood while carrying a terminal diazene; that substitution is not shown to be chemically necessary.

per_task.generated_character: The trajectory is dominated by large, aromatic diaryl fused dione heterocycles, with a second upper-score family of biaryl chromenones bearing nitriles. The aromatic periphery acquires imines, carbodiimide-type cumulated nitrogen functionality, oxime-like chains, nitrogen-nitrogen links and fluorine bonded directly to nitrogen or oxygen. Evaluation 254 combines a fused dione with imine and fluorinated nitrogen/oxygen appendages; 249 carries similarly decorated aromatic surfaces on the chromenone family. The last molecules also contain oxygen-oxygen chains ending in fluorine. Mean SMILES length is 65.6, aromatic_atom_rate is 1.0, halogen_rate is 0.9621 and cumulated_double_bond_rate is 0.631. The underlying ring systems are recognizable, but the dense combinations of heteroatom-halogen and unsaturated nitrogen functionality make the complete products questionable synthetic endpoints.
liabilities: Nitrogen-fluorinated imines/carbodiimides and oxygen-fluorinated oxime-like groups are chemically different from routine aryl fluorination. Their repeated combination raises handling and functional-group compatibility concerns.
The final oxygen-oxygen chains ending in fluorine add peroxide-like connectivity. The acceptable recorded scores do not demonstrate stability or an executable synthesis for these combinations.

Repeated C=N and N=N units introduce geometric possibilities that are unspecified in the cited strings. Cumulated functionality is not automatically implausible in isolation, but these densely heteroatom-substituted combinations are not supported by synthesis evidence.
missing_features: Chemically ordinary realizations of the same aromatic polar substitution patterns are thin in the current high-score excerpt: nitrogen and oxygen are repeatedly supplied through fluorinated unsaturated chains. The missing comparison is a stable, compact functional-group arrangement at those sites, not simply more nitrogen or fluorine.

The upper-score series provides little evidence of new cyclic linkers or changed ring heteroatom patterns. Multiple inherited aromatic families occur, but their pendant-chain elaboration does not establish broad exploration of alternative ring architecture.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The initial diaryl dione at 7 scores 0.548381; the elaborated relative at 254 scores 0.589489. The chromenone/nitrile analogue at 249 reaches 0.588545, so the upper region is not restricted to the dione core. The pyrazoline/phenol derivative at 20 scores 0.535497, and the quinoline/phenoxy/piperidine derivative at 18 scores 0.536296. Within the late dione sequence, changing an oxygen-chain endpoint at 298 to the oxygen/nitrogen chain at 299 accompanies 0.580425 versus 0.587001. These observations show local tolerance of elaborate polar aromatic decoration; they do not isolate a requirement for any reactive bond. The Parent maximum was 0.583606 on a diaryl dione decorated with amino, thioether and azo functionality. The current upper-score chemistry shifts toward fluorinated imine/oxime/carbodiimide appendages while retaining a familiar ring family.

per_task.generated_character: These are large, heavily substituted biphenyl/arylsulfonyl-pyrrolidine compounds with flexible secondary or tertiary aliphatic amine linkers. The pyrrolidine nitrogen remains sulfonylated; the visibly available amine centres are elsewhere, including linker nitrogens and aniline groups. The maximum at 286 combines an aniline-bearing biphenyl, a tertiary amine carrying a dibromomethyl group, a chlorinated allylic branch, an aryl thiol and a terminal disulfanyl/persulfide group. The other upper molecules repeatedly carry brominated carbon groups, thiols, persulfides and sometimes oxygen-bromine appendages. Mean SMILES length is 81.5, aromatic_atom_rate is 0.9759 and halogen_rate is 0.9517. The core sulfonamide/amine chemistry is familiar, but the cumulative size and unusual peripheral combinations make these questionable complete synthetic targets.
liabilities: Brominated amine substituents, chlorinated allylic branches and extensive aromatic halogenation create a bulky, chemically demanding periphery. Direct O-Br groups in some upper examples are distinct from ordinary carbon-bound bromine.
Aryl thiols, terminal persulfides and mixed sulfur chains add compatibility and oxidation-state concerns. These motifs should not be summarized merely as conventional thioethers or sulfones.

Multiple flexible connections, crowded substituted saturated centres and unspecified stereochemistry complicate molecular identity and synthesis. The recorded task scalar is not a measurement of affinity or selectivity.
missing_features: The dominant family does not independently explore nitrogen electronic state and placement: its cyclic nitrogen stays sulfonylated while added basic centres occupy external linkers. A conventional unsulfonylated cyclic amine in this same geometric setting is not shown; its value cannot be inferred from the low-scoring amine-containing alternative scaffold.

Chemically simple matched alternatives to the dibromomethyl-, persulfide- and oxygen-bromine-bearing periphery are not well represented in the cited upper set. An ordinary secondary amine connector does occur at 214, so the gap is retaining useful amine geometry while independently reducing peripheral liabilities.

The substituted saturated ring and branched linker centres are not stereochemically specified, and explicitly charged alternatives are absent from the proposal strings. Evaluation-side protonation or conformer preparation is not documented here.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The initial acid/amide-linked arylsulfonyl pyrrolidine at 10 scores 0.0190412. The amine-linked sulfur-rich member at 210 scores 0.187213 and the related compound at 286 reaches 0.284516. Several structural features change together, so neither sulfur addition nor amide/acid removal can be assigned that gain independently. The bromophenyl diaryl dione at 133 scores 0.000747521. The initial quinoline/piperidine at 6 scores 0.000378699 despite containing an ordinary tertiary cyclic amine, showing that amine presence alone does not explain the gradient. The late pair 296 and 297 changes a larger dithiol-containing side branch to a directly attached thiol on the saturated ring, with scores 0.0991265 and 0.192606. Thus additional sulfur-bearing bulk is not uniformly favorable. The Parent maximum of 0.189601 had a chlorinated enamine linker on the same broad arylsulfonyl-pyrrolidine family. The current upper series emphasizes aliphatic amines and sulfur/bromine-rich decoration; no binding pose or specific receptor interaction is established by these records.

per_task.generated_character: The upper-score chemistry is comparatively conventional: alkylated diaryl fused diones bearing ordinary carbonyls, phenols and short hydrocarbon substituents, alongside quinoline/phenoxy conjugates of N-methyl piperidines. Evaluation 92 combines the fused dione with propyl and ethyl substitution, a phenol and an aldehyde. Evaluation 221 has a quinoline ether, an aniline-linked piperidine, a ketone and an aldehyde. The wider proposal set also repeatedly retains the arylsulfonyl pyrrolidine/acid family. These are medium-to-large aromatic molecules; mean SMILES length is 68.3, aromatic_atom_rate is 1.0, halogen_rate is 0.4862 and cumulated_double_bond_rate is 0.0. The principal high-score structures look plausible as medicinal-chemistry starting points in outline, although aldehydes and some bulky alkyl elaborations still need scrutiny.
liabilities: Several upper examples carry aldehydes, which leave electrophilicity and chemical-compatibility questions even when the rest of the molecule uses familiar functionality.
Longer alkyl branches add flexible hydrophobic material without a monotonic recorded benefit. The final butyl/pentyl pair makes that limitation visible.
The piperidine-containing examples leave stereochemical configurations unspecified. Earlier N-O-rich variants elsewhere in the trajectory are less ordinary than the principal alkyl/carbonyl series.
missing_features: The high-score quinoline/piperidine entries do not supply a matched set of less reactive alternatives to their aldehydes. The high-scoring dione methyl ester shows that an aldehyde is not universally required in the observed upper range, but transferring that substitution between frameworks remains untested.

Alternative ring arrangements and defined configurations of substituted piperidines are not represented by the cited upper-score molecules. The modest positional and chain-length gradients do not identify a specific absent target pharmacophore.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The initial diaryl dione at 7 scores 0.167839; the alkyl/aldehyde-substituted member at 92 scores 0.183910. The quinoline/piperidine example at 221 scores 0.181769, and the dione methyl ester at 239 scores 0.181135. The modified biphenyl/pyran carboxamide at 30 scores 0.105623. Ordinary functional groups are therefore compatible with both higher and lower scores; their arrangement on the ring framework matters. The late dione pair 295 and 296 differs in the position of a phenyl methyl substituent and scores 0.175187 versus 0.180579. Extending the peripheral butyl chain of 299 to the pentyl chain of 300 changes 0.177211 to 0.173640. These are direct examples of position and chain length mattering without a general reward for molecular growth. The Parent maximum was 0.175888 in a quinoline/piperidine aldehyde series. The current maximum lies in the diaryl dione family, while ordinary alkyl/ether/carbonyl chemistry remains present in both panels.

per_task.generated_character: The strongest observed molecules are densely oxygenated, nonaromatic polyacetals resembling protected carbohydrate frameworks. Their periphery contains direct S-F groups, alkynes ending in sulfur-fluorine functionality, N-Cl groups and aldehydes. Evaluation 220 has that combination on the polyacetal framework. Aromatic diaryl diones remain common in the trajectory, and evaluation 129 reaches the upper excerpt with fluoroalkynyl and carbonyl substituents. Mean SMILES length is 57.8, aromatic_atom_rate is 0.6448 and halogen_rate is 0.8034: the high polyacetals must not be mistaken for a wholly nonaromatic proposal set. The ring frameworks are recognizable, but their densely substituted heteroatom-halogen and alkynyl periphery is questionable as a stable, isolable synthetic series.
liabilities: Direct sulfur-fluorine and nitrogen-chlorine bonds, fluoroalkynes and alkynyl sulfur-fluorine groups are unusual medicinal substituents whose mutual compatibility is not established by a valid molecular graph.
The crowded polyacetal framework would require stereochemical and synthetic control. The proposal strings provide neither explicit configurations nor evidence of an executable route.

The final aromatic compounds continue to combine sulfur-containing appendages with N-Cl and nitrogen-nitrogen functionality. Their very small scores do not rescue the chemical plausibility of those combinations.
missing_features: The upper polyacetal series lacks demonstrated chemically ordinary replacements that retain its locally favorable heteroatom and unsaturation arrangement without direct S-F/N-Cl or haloalkynyl endpoints. Whether such a replacement preserves any score is unknown.

Configurations of the numerous substituted oxygen-bearing centres are absent. The records therefore do not establish a stereochemically defined series, despite the complexity of the underlying frameworks.

No specific absent pharmacophore follows from these scores: both aromatic and nonaromatic families can enter the upper excerpt, while closely related heteroatom-rich derivatives can score extremely poorly. Missing target chemistry cannot be assigned from the task name.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The initial polyacetal at 4 scores 2.54690e-05; the substituted relative at 220 scores 0.0317402. The initial aromatic dione at 7 scores 0.00209445, and the fluoroalkynyl dione at 129 scores 0.0158795. The gradient therefore admits more than one ring family. The aryl pyrazoline/thioamide carrying sulfur-fluorine and fluoroalkyl substitution at 184 scores only 3.08411e-39, while the nitrogen-chain-decorated polyacetal at 20 scores 1.16030e-25. Neither sulfur/fluorine presence nor the polyacetal framework alone explains the higher values. In the late polyacetal sequence 295-297, changing the alkyne endpoint gives 0.00159344 for the nitrogen-chlorine variant, 0.00751374 for the sulfur-fluorine variant and 4.65983e-05 for the aldehyde variant. Those matched local examples show a sharp dependence on the particular peripheral group. The Parent maximum was 0.0881235 on a polyacetal decorated with terminal thiocarbonyls, an aldehyde and a trichloromethyl group. The current upper chemistry shifts to S-F/N-Cl/alkynyl decoration and a lower recorded maximum; neither panel supplies evidence of a conventional stable endpoint.

transferable_gaps.evidence: High-score examples repeatedly carry direct N-F, O-F, S-F, N-Cl or O-Br bonds, nitrogen/oxygen chains, terminal persulfides and haloalkynes. One proposal set has cumulated_double_bond_rate 0.631 and halogen_rate 0.9621; another has halogen_rate 0.9517. At the same time, a simple indole carboxamide scores 0.352934 and an alkylated diaryl dione scores 0.183910 in their respective trajectories. The molecules demonstrate conventional alternatives, but their polar substituents often become elaborate heteroatom chains rather than independently varied familiar functional groups.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator does not reliably express new polar functionality as chemically compatible, conventional local groups.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: A task-agnostic generator needs local chemical-environment and compatibility control that keeps ordinary amines, amides, ethers, carbonyls and appropriately stabilized sulfur groups available as alternatives. Separate halogen attached to carbon from halogen attached to a heteroatom, and avoid treating equal atom inventories as chemically interchangeable. Preserve comparable ordinary substitutions for feedback to assess; the observed records do not justify declaring a universal score benefit for any functional-group restriction.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Ring_closure_rate is 1.0 for every proposal set, yet the cited upper molecules remain recognizable derivatives of initial indoles, fused diones, chromenones, arylsulfonyl pyrrolidines, quinoline/piperidine conjugates or polyacetals. The comparison with the Parent mainly changes pendant groups and the prominence of these same families. Ring abundance therefore does not establish broad coverage of alternative cyclic connectivity or ring heteroatom placement.
transferable_gaps.gap: The output demonstrates abundant inherited rings but limited exploration of substantially different cyclic architecture.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Broader chemical coverage would require a generator domain that can vary ring connectivity, ring heteroatom arrangement and the links between ring units while preserving feasible chemistry. This is a coverage gap inferred from the products, not evidence that a particular unseen ring system improves an objective.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Stereocentre_rate and charged_rate are both 0.0 on every task. The actual products nevertheless include substituted piperidines and pyrrolidines, branched amine linkers and elaborate polyacetals with potential stereogenic centres, as well as ionizable amines and acids. Cited imine and diazene products also leave geometric alternatives unspecified. These observations establish absent submitted-state annotations, not absence of stereochemistry or ionization in solution; evaluation-side preparation is not shown.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generated structures leave stereochemical and ionization-state alternatives unresolved.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Where the candidate contract permits, express chemically justified stereoisomers and ionization states explicitly and preserve those distinctions in candidate identity. Base state handling on generic chemical rules and observed feedback, without assuming that an annotation itself improves a score.

nodes.method_name: Inverse-QSAR: mixed-integer de novo molecular construction
nodes.method_thesis: Anchor the method in inverse-QSAR through coupled linear regression and mixed-integer graph construction. [Zhu et al., Sections 1, 3 and 4](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/FBL/27/6/10.31083/j.fbl2706188) encode both a molecular descriptor function and a learned predictor in a program that constructs a graph satisfying structural specifications. Our benchmark adaptation fits a regularized linear score model only to the current objective's accepted observations, using atom-type, degree and typed-bond counts that can be represented exactly by integer constraints. For each proposal, take a scored molecule, choose a bounded editable peripheral region and retain its connected surrounding context. Represent replacement atom identities, bond orders and attachment choices as discrete variables, with connectivity, valence and descriptor-consistency constraints. Maximize the fitted scalar prediction over these variables instead of solving the paper's fixed target-interval problem. A feasible integer assignment supplies the new molecular graph directly. Validate the actual graph and recompute its descriptors before submission; exclude repeated assignments and retry construction when canonical identity is duplicate or invalid. Vary contexts and editable regions as feedback accumulates, and continue construction until the announced batch is filled. Use bounded subproblems and feasible solver incumbents rather than requiring a proof of global optimality for every proposal. The root needs no generative checkpoint or external labels. It constructs atom and bond combinations, without a corpus molecule pool, stored-fragment retrieval or the paper's subsequent isomer-enumeration stage. Each objective starts with clean scored and fitted state. The hypothesis is that jointly enforcing realizable structure while optimizing a task-local prediction concentrates evaluations on improving molecules and raises the mean of independent final Top-1 scores. Exact descriptor realization cannot compensate for an inaccurate predictor; both predictive usefulness and sufficient construction throughput remain unproven.

approach.method_basis: The Parent breeds fresh molecular graphs from a bounded population of accepted high-scoring molecules. Its connected-fragment crossover and local edits include a retained formula-preserving exchange of aromatic nitrogen positions, and stable identity checks admit a surplus of novel candidates. A Gaussian process trained on the full accepted-score archive compares integer counts of local molecular environments using generalized Tanimoto covariance. For each batch slot, the Parent takes a separate correlated posterior draw and submits its best available molecule. Accepted feedback updates both the breeding population and the prediction archive.
approach.novelty: Choose each molecule for the additional predicted best score it brings to the batch. Pair the existing full posterior draws with their reflections around the unchanged predictive mean, then greedily cover high scores across this shared panel. A molecule that mostly repeats peaks already covered by earlier choices has little marginal value. The earlier batch-coordination sibling conditioned pending molecules to their predicted means and reduced sampling variance; this rule keeps that variation and compares marginal batch utility instead. Other siblings changed breeding, graph edits, identity admission or the predictive model. None of the supplied siblings has tested this expected-batch-maximum allocation rule. Its usefulness depends on actual evaluated outcomes, not on wider chemical coverage.

nodes.hypothesis: Allocate the batch by greedy marginal expected-maximum gain over a shared antithetic panel of the inherited joint posterior draws, so each selection accounts for the score peaks already covered by earlier selections.

finding_summary.headline: Batch-maximum allocation changes choices but lowers mean final score by 0.0161
finding_summary.insights:
This establishes a real effect from later marginal allocation, beyond the first mean-ranked choice or antithetic arithmetic alone. It also shows that correctly increasing the model's sampled batch maximum is insufficient to improve the final best evaluated score on this panel. The original predictive model and random draws remain intact on identical inputs, narrowing the explanation to the changed allocation and its subsequent feedback trajectory. Unavailable alternative molecules have no oracle labels, so same-pool utility comparisons cannot identify which individual replacements caused the score losses.

The objective rewards a batch's maximum without requiring it to beat the incumbent, and twenty dependent antithetic scenarios approximate the model's tails. Together with the selected-stream uncertainty undercoverage, these leave a concrete mismatch between acquisition utility and useful search progress. More incumbent updates and lower selected-stream prediction error also failed to produce a higher endpoint: improvement frequency and average prediction accuracy do not measure how far the search advances. Because the later selected molecules differ, the MSE comparison does not establish better prediction or calibration on common molecules. An incumbent-relative utility or a separately tested correction to predictive uncertainty is worth distinguishing next; neither is established as the cause here. On the Child's fixed pools, mean count-fingerprint similarity falls from 0.6860 to 0.6810, yet distinct nonempty cores per batch also fall from 6.846 to 6.641 and acyclic selections rise from 104 to 145. Similarity instead increases when the same rule is applied to the Parent's pools. This separates lower pairwise similarity from broader core coverage and shows that the secondary effects depend on the pool.

The molecular assessment finds useful polar motifs within ring-rich families alongside reactive heteroatom bonds, constrained ring systems and unspecified stereochemistry. Smaller molecules do not consistently give better endpoints. Allocation preserves those chemical limitations, so the internal utility increase supplies no evidence of improved feasibility or broadly useful chemistry.
finding_summary.results:
The rule changes 431 of 435 submitted batch sets versus independent posterior draws on the same pools. All 3,596 later choices with positive marginal value follow the registered maximizer; 3,256 differ from the original draw's choice on the identical available mask. Another 319 positions use the registered mean completion after sampled gains reach exactly zero. Average maximum over the shared scenario panel rises by 0.00617, with 396 pools improving and 0 declining. This is internal sampled utility.

Evaluated three-seed mean final score falls from 0.57434 to 0.55824, a change of -0.01610 against the registered +0.002 target. Seed changes are −0.03008, +0.01124 and −0.02948; 8 of 15 task/seed endpoints decline, and every task's mean declines. The largest mean loss is sitagliptin at 0.05362. Strict improvements over the best generating parent are 621/4,350 versus 624/4,350, and incumbent improvements are 250 versus 241. Mean evaluated batch maximum falls from 0.48731 to 0.45721, while prediction MSE on each run's selected stream falls from 0.01127 to 0.00924. Nominal 95% latent intervals cover 77.86% of selected scores versus 76.92% for the Parent. All evaluations complete; no numerical fallback occurs.
